items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary about India. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices the people in short dramatised scenes (merchants, engineers, scholars, servants, kings, emperors, sultans, officials, soldiers): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce Indian names and places naturally, the way an Indian speaker would. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy. PRONUNCIATION (say these names exactly like this, stress on the capital syllables): Harappa = huh-RUP-uh; Meerut = MEE-rut; Bahadur Shah Zafar = buh-HAA-door shaah ZUF-ur; Lakshmibai = LUCK-shmee-bye; Jhansi = JHAAN-see; champo = CHUM-poh; Dadabhai Naoroji = DAA-daa-bye NOW-roh-jee.
lines: In eighteen fifty-seven, the Company gave its Indian soldiers a new rifle. To load it, you had to bite open a paper cartridge. A rumour spread like fire: the cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike.
At Meerut, soldiers who refused them were jailed. Their comrades rose up, freed them, and marched to Delhi, where they declared the old Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, ruler of India again.
The revolt spread across the north. And one of its fiercest leaders was a young widow the Company had tried to retire.
Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi. When her husband died, the Company refused to accept her adopted son as heir, and simply took her kingdom. She was handed a pension and told to step aside.
In eighteen fifty-seven, she stepped back in. She led her troops on horseback, and died fighting, in her late twenties. She became the most famous face of the revolt.
The British crushed the rising with terrible brutality. Whole villages were burned. Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Burma. The Mughal dynasty, after three hundred and thirty years, was over.
London decided the Company could not be trusted with India anymore. In eighteen fifty-eight, the British Crown took over directly. The Raj had begun.
Your Majesty, India is now ruled by the Crown.
Then I shall need a new title.
She got it, in eighteen seventy-six.
India gave Britain smaller things too. In eighteen fourteen, an Indian businessman opened a bath house in Brighton offering a head massage called champo. Today you'd call it shampoo.
Under the Raj, India got railways. Remember those bricks from Harappa? Same railway age. The tracks ran mainly to carry raw cotton to the ports, and British factory cloth back in.
Think about that. India, the land of calico and chintz, the land that once dressed half the world, now bought its cloth from Manchester.
And the famines kept coming. In the Great Famine of eighteen seventy-six, millions died while grain was still being exported.

Then an Indian thinker named Dadabhai Naoroji sat down with the numbers. Remember Pliny, the Roman who complained that India drained Rome of its gold? Naoroji made the same complaint, the other way round. He called it the drain of wealth: India's money flowing out to Britain, year after year.

But the British also built schools, newspapers and universities. And in them, a new generation of Indians learned exactly how to argue with an empire. One of them was a young lawyer, about to be thrown off a train.

lines: June, eighteen ninety-three. A young Indian lawyer is sitting in a first-class compartment on a train in South Africa. He has a valid ticket. A white passenger complains. At Pietermaritzburg station, he is thrown off the train.
He spent that night shivering in the station waiting room, deciding whether to go home or to fight. He stayed, and fought, for more than twenty years.
His name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. When he came home to India in nineteen fifteen, people would come to call him Mahatma, "great soul".
His weapon was satyagraha: holding on to the truth, and resisting without violence.

In nineteen nineteen, in Amritsar, thousands of people gathered peacefully in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh. A British general blocked the exit and ordered his troops to fire into the crowd. They fired until they ran out of bullets. The official count was three hundred and seventy-nine dead. Indian estimates were over a thousand.
After Amritsar, millions of Indians who had trusted the British stopped trusting them.
And Gandhi chose the most unlikely weapon in history. Remember that Indian cloth? Remember Manchester? Gandhi told Indians to burn foreign cloth, and spin their own.

He sat at a spinning wheel, the charkha, every day, and wore rough homespun cotton called khadi. The spinning wheel went onto the freedom movement's flag. The cloth that had once made India rich would now help set it free.
In nineteen thirty, he picked an even stranger target: salt. The British taxed it, and Indians were banned from making their own. So Gandhi walked to the sea.
Mr Gandhi, what exactly are you doing?
Then arrest me. And the thousands behind me.
[looking at the crowd, then his notebook] I'll need a bigger notebook.
The Salt March covered about three hundred and eighty kilometres in twenty-four days, and newspapers around the world followed every step.

Not everyone believed in non-violence. Bhagat Singh took up arms, and was hanged at twenty-three. Subhas Chandra Bose raised an army with Japan's help. And Dr B R Ambedkar, born into a so-called untouchable caste, fought for India's most oppressed people.

In the Second World War, about two and a half million Indian soldiers fought for Britain, the largest volunteer army in history. Meanwhile, in nineteen forty-three, a famine in Bengal killed around three million people.
By the end of the war, Britain was broke and exhausted. It could no longer hold on to India.
Freedom was coming. But it was not coming whole.

lines: The British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe had never been to India. In the summer of nineteen forty-seven, he was given about five weeks to draw the line that would split it.
The Congress and the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, could not agree on one country. The League demanded a separate homeland for Muslims: Pakistan. Britain agreed to divide the land.
Sir, the census figures for the Punjab.
[wiping his glasses] And how long do I have?

At midnight on the fifteenth of August, nineteen forty-seven, India became free. In Delhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, told the assembly that at the stroke of midnight, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom.
But Radcliffe's line was only announced two days later. Across Punjab and Bengal, millions of people woke up on the "wrong" side of a border they had never seen.

What followed was one of the largest migrations in human history. Somewhere between ten and twenty million people were forced from their homes. Trains arrived carrying only the dead. Estimates of those killed range from two hundred thousand to two million.
Gandhi spent Independence Day not in Delhi, but in Calcutta, fasting to stop the killing. Five months later, on the thirtieth of January, nineteen forty-eight, he was shot dead by a Hindu extremist.

India had another enormous problem. More than five hundred and sixty princely states, each ruled by its own maharaja or nawab, had to choose where to go. The man in charge was the Home Minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
My family has ruled here for three hundred years.
And India would be honoured to keep you comfortable for three hundred more.
Most signed. Hyderabad held out until the Indian army moved in. Kashmir's ruler signed after raiders from Pakistan invaded, and the first war between India and Pakistan began.

Then India wrote its rules. A committee led by Dr Ambedkar drafted the Constitution, the longest written constitution of any country. It came into force on the twenty-sixth of January, nineteen fifty: Republic Day.

And remember Ashoka's wheel? When India chose its national flag, there were two wheels in the running. Gandhi's spinning wheel had been on the freedom flag for years. But in July nineteen forty-seven, the Constituent Assembly replaced it with the Ashoka Chakra. The emperor who apologised in stone, back at the centre of the flag, after two thousand years.

The new republic also did something many rich democracies took centuries to do: it gave every adult the vote, from day one. In the first election, about a hundred and seventy million people were eligible, and most of them could not read. So every party got a picture symbol.
The biggest election the world had ever seen, run on pictures.
India was free. It was also poor. And it was about to find out how close to broke a country can get.

lines: The young republic had a rough start. It lost a border war with China in nineteen sixty-two, and fought Pakistan in nineteen sixty-five. By the mid-sixties, India was so short of food that it depended on grain shipments from America.
Then came the Green Revolution: new high-yield wheat and rice, irrigation and fertiliser. Within about a decade, India could feed itself.
In nineteen seventy-one, India backed the independence struggle in East Pakistan and won a short war. A new country was born: Bangladesh.

In nineteen seventy-five, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared an Emergency. Elections were suspended, opponents jailed, newspapers censored. And when she finally called elections, the voters, the same voters of the picture symbols, threw her out.
For most of these years, India's economy was tightly controlled. You needed government permission to make almost anything. People called it the Licence Raj.
In nineteen ninety-one, it all came to a head. India nearly ran out of money. Its foreign reserves could pay for only about three weeks of imports.
To get an emergency loan, the government did something unthinkable. It flew forty-seven tonnes of its own gold to the Bank of England.
Remember Mahmud's camels, carrying India's gold away? Remember Naoroji's drain? Now India had to send its own gold to London.
Cargo: forty-seven tonnes of gold. Destination: London.
Wait... didn't the British take enough already?
This time, we're getting it back.

And they did. Because that crisis forced a revolution. A quiet economist named Manmohan Singh, the new finance minister, stood up in Parliament and quoted Victor Hugo: no power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come.
India opened up. Lower taxes on imports. Private companies welcome. Foreign investment allowed. Growth took off, and software companies in Bengaluru and Hyderabad began serving the whole world.
In two thousand fourteen, India reached Mars on its very first try, for about seventy-four million dollars. Less than the Hollywood space film Gravity cost to make.
In two thousand twenty-three, Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to land near the Moon's south pole. That same year, India became the most populous country on Earth.
Narendra Modi has been Prime Minister since two thousand fourteen. Today India is the world's fifth-largest economy, and the IMF expects it to pass Japan next year.
To be fair, it still has a long way to go. Hundreds of millions still earn very little. Good jobs are scarce for the young. And critics worry about pressure on the press and on religious minorities.
But the Golden Bird is climbing again.
So think about everyone who came to take something from this land. Alexander. The Kushans. Mahmud. Ghori. Timur. Babur. Nadir Shah. A company from London.
Think about everything they carried off: gold on camels, a peacock throne, a diamond that now sits in the Tower of London, and a drain of wealth that ran for two hundred years.
And now, the question from the start. Why did almost every robber end up staying?
Here's the answer. India's wealth could always be carried away. India itself never could.

The Kushans became champions of Indian Buddhism. The sultans' soldiers gave India Urdu and qawwali. Babur arrived missing his melons, and his great-great-grandson built the Taj Mahal. Again and again, the invaders ended up eating India's food, speaking its languages, and building its monuments.
Only one never moved in. It ruled from an office in London, and it sent the money home. By the time it left, India's share of the world had fallen to about four percent.‡
Remember that sailor at Calicut, more than five hundred years ago? He came for spices, and for cloth so fine that Europe named it after the port where he stood.
Today, the world is coming back to buy from India again. Its software, its medicines, and yes, its cloth. India is once again one of the biggest cloth-makers on Earth.
The Golden Bird lost its gold more times than anyone can count. It never lost itself.
